items.item: Prepare asks every participant to durably promise it can commit; once every participant votes yes, the coordinator durably logs the decision and only then announces it to everyone.

at.step: Reveal: what a yes vote actually promises

items.item: A participant that voted yes is in doubt: the final outcome could be either commit or abort, and it cannot discover which on its own, so it must hold its locks until the announcement arrives.

at.step: Reveal: in doubt, and why that means holding the locks

items.item: If the coordinator crashes after logging its decision but before announcing it, every participant that voted yes blocks indefinitely, holding its locks, until the coordinator (or its decision) becomes reachable again.

at.step: Hook: the coordinator decided, then vanished before telling anyone

items.item: Three-phase commit adds a pre-commit phase so a participant that received it can finish without waiting for a crashed coordinator, but this rescue depends on a timeout correctly meaning the coordinator crashed, which only holds when the network is not partitioned.

at.step: Reveal: 3PC's extra phase, and what it still needs to be true

items.item: Paxos maintains a single consistent decision even if multiple processes each believe themselves the leader, which traditional three-phase commit protocols do not: there, multiple coordinators arising from a partition can lead to inconsistency.

at.step: Reveal: 3PC's extra phase, and what it still needs to be true

items.item: Paxos Commit runs a Paxos consensus instance on each participant's commit/abort vote, using 2F + 1 coordinators and making progress once F + 1 of them are working, so the decision survives losing a minority of the coordinator group rather than depending on one machine.

at.step: Reveal: Paxos Commit — a vote the coordinator's death can't erase

items.item: Classic Two-Phase Commit is the special F = 0 case of Paxos Commit: the same protocol with no fault tolerance built into the coordinator role at all.

at.step: Reveal: Paxos Commit — a vote the coordinator's death can't erase

items.item: Spanner stores each transaction manager's state inside its own underlying Paxos group, so the state survives losing that group's leader; CockroachDB's Parallel Commits runs every participant's consensus round trip concurrently rather than in sequence, roughly halving commit latency.

at.step: Reveal: where production places the consensus group

items.item: A saga replaces one atomic transaction with a sequence of local steps, each paired with a compensating action that can undo it, trading atomicity for eventual consistency managed at the application level; the transactional outbox pattern commits an event in the same local write and lets a separate process deliver it later.

at.step: Reveal: sagas and the outbox, named and left for elsewhere

items.item: Replicating the coordinator's decision through a consensus log removes exactly the single-machine failure that caused blocking before; a participant can still end up in doubt from its own crash, a lost message, or the decision-replicating group itself losing its majority.
